sections.content: If you own rental property, 2026 is a year you need to circle on your calendar. The generous bonus depreciation rules that let investors write off large chunks of a property's cost in year one are winding down — and the 2026 rules mark a pivotal shift that could cost you tens of thousands of dollars if you are not prepared. Understanding the bonus depreciation on rental property 2026 rules now gives you time to make smart moves before the phase-out is complete.
What Is Bonus Depreciation and Why Does It Matter for Rental Property?

Bonus depreciation is a tax provision that lets real estate investors deduct a large percentage of the cost of certain assets in the year they are placed in service, rather than spreading those deductions out over decades. Under normal depreciation rules, a residential rental property is depreciated over 27.5 years. That means a $275,000 building gives you roughly $10,000 in depreciation deductions each year. Bonus depreciation is different — it lets you front-load those deductions on qualifying components of the property, which can dramatically reduce your taxable income in a single year.

This provision was turbocharged by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA), which temporarily raised the bonus depreciation rate to 100%. That meant investors could write off the full cost of qualifying personal property and land improvements in year one. It was a game-changer for rental property owners who used cost segregation studies to identify short-life assets inside their buildings.
The Bonus Depreciation Phase-Out Schedule: Where Do We Stand?

The 100% bonus depreciation era is officially over, but the deduction has not disappeared entirely. The TCJA included a built-in phase-out schedule that reduces the percentage each year. Here is where the numbers land:

items: 2022: 100% bonus depreciation (final year of full deduction)
2023: 80% bonus depreciation
2024: 60% bonus depreciation
2025: 40% bonus depreciation
2026: 20% bonus depreciation
2027 and beyond: 0% bonus depreciation (unless Congress acts)

sections.content: That means in 2026, if you identify $100,000 in qualifying assets through a cost segregation study, you can only write off $20,000 immediately. The remaining $80,000 gets depreciated over shorter standard lives of 5, 7, or 15 years depending on the asset category. It is still better than 27.5-year straight-line depreciation, but it is a far cry from the 100% deductions investors enjoyed just a few years ago.

Pro Tip: If you are planning to buy a rental property in 2025, closing before December 31, 2025 locks in the 40% bonus depreciation rate — double what you will get if you wait until 2026. Timing your acquisitions around the phase-out schedule can be worth thousands in tax savings.
What Qualifies for Bonus Depreciation on Rental Property?

Not every part of your rental property qualifies for bonus depreciation. The building structure itself — the walls, roof, and foundation — must be depreciated over 27.5 years for residential property. However, many components inside and around the property have much shorter useful lives and can qualify for bonus depreciation treatment.
Common Qualifying Assets Identified Through Cost Segregation

items: 5-year property: Carpeting, appliances, certain fixtures, decorative elements
7-year property: Office furniture and equipment used in property management
15-year property: Landscaping, parking lots, sidewalks, fencing, outdoor lighting
Qualified Improvement Property (QIP): Interior improvements to nonresidential buildings

sections.content: A cost segregation study is an engineering-based analysis that dissects your property and assigns each component to the correct depreciation category. For a $500,000 rental property, a cost segregation study might identify $80,000 to $120,000 in short-life assets. In 2025 at 40% bonus depreciation, that could mean an immediate deduction of $32,000 to $48,000 — compared to roughly $1,455 per year if those same assets were lumped into 27.5-year depreciation.
How Bonus Depreciation Works in Practice: A Real Example

Let us say you purchase a rental duplex in Dallas, TX for $420,000 in early 2026. You hire a cost segregation firm for $4,000, and they identify $95,000 in qualifying 5-year and 15-year property. Here is what your first-year deductions look like under the 2026 bonus depreciation rules:

items: Qualifying assets identified: $95,000
2026 bonus depreciation rate: 20%
Immediate bonus depreciation deduction: $19,000
Remaining $76,000 depreciated over 5 or 15 years (adds roughly $10,000-$15,000 more per year)
Standard 27.5-year depreciation on remaining building value: approximately $11,818 per year
Total first-year depreciation deduction: approximately $30,000 to $35,000

sections.content: If your marginal tax rate is 32%, that $35,000 deduction saves you roughly $11,200 in federal taxes in year one. That is real money that can be reinvested into your next deal. "Depreciation is the best tax shelter available to real estate investors. Even as bonus depreciation phases out, a well-executed cost segregation study will beat straight-line depreciation every single time." — Common wisdom among experienced real estate CPAs
Will Congress Restore 100% Bonus Depreciation?

This is the question every real estate investor is asking. There has been bipartisan interest in extending or restoring 100% bonus depreciation, and various tax reform proposals have floated through Congress in recent years. The Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act of 2024 was one such effort that included bonus depreciation provisions, though it did not ultimately pass the Senate in the form needed. As of the time of writing, investors should plan around current law — meaning the 20% rate in 2026 and zero in 2027 — while staying alert to legislative developments. Do not make major acquisition or renovation decisions based on a rule change that has not yet been signed into law.
Strategies to Maximize Your Deductions Under the 2026 Rules
1. Accelerate Acquisitions Where Possible

Properties placed in service in 2025 capture the 40% rate. Closing in early 2025 rather than waiting until 2026 is worth twice the immediate bonus depreciation deduction on qualifying assets. If you are actively looking for rental properties in high-growth markets like [Dallas, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), moving quickly on acquisitions has a real tax advantage beyond just locking in a good price.
2. Invest in Capital Improvements Before Year-End

Major renovations to existing rentals can also generate qualifying assets for bonus depreciation. Replacing flooring, upgrading appliances, or adding a new fence all create components that may qualify. Timing those improvements before December 31 of a given year ensures you capture that year's bonus depreciation rate.
3. Order a Cost Segregation Study Even at Lower Rates

Many investors assume cost segregation is only worth doing at 100% bonus depreciation. That is not true. Even at 20% in 2026, the time value of money means you are better off with deductions today than deductions spread over 27.5 years. A study on a $600,000 property can easily deliver $5,000 to $15,000 in additional first-year tax savings even under current rules.
4. Model Your Cash Flow with Depreciation in Mind

Your after-tax cash flow is what really matters. Use the free [Cash Flow Calculator at aiwholesail.com](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/cash-flow-calculator) to model how depreciation deductions affect your net returns on a potential deal. Plugging in your projected depreciation helps you see whether a deal makes sense on a true after-tax basis — not just on paper rents and expenses.

Pro Tip: Bonus depreciation deductions can create a paper loss even when your rental property generates positive cash flow. Depending on your income level and whether you qualify as a real estate professional under IRS rules, those losses may offset ordinary income from your W-2 or business — amplifying your tax savings significantly.
Passive Activity Rules and Real Estate Professional Status

One important caveat: bonus depreciation deductions on rental property are generally considered passive losses. If your adjusted gross income exceeds $150,000, you typically cannot use passive losses to offset ordinary income — they carry forward until you sell the property or generate passive income. However, if you or your spouse qualifies as a real estate professional under IRS rules (meaning you spend more than 750 hours per year in real estate activities and it represents more than half your working hours), those losses become non-passive and can offset any type of income. This is a powerful strategy, but it requires careful documentation and a conversation with a qualified CPA.

Key Takeaways for Rental Property Investors in 2026

items: The 2026 bonus depreciation rate is 20% — down from 40% in 2025 and 60% in 2024
Bonus depreciation applies to qualifying personal property and land improvements, not the building structure
Cost segregation studies are still worth doing even at the 20% rate
Closing deals in 2025 rather than 2026 captures a higher deduction rate
Real estate professional status can unlock the full tax benefit of paper losses
Monitor Congress for potential legislative changes that could restore higher bonus depreciation rates
Always model after-tax cash flow, not just gross rental income, when evaluating deals
